blocks.title: Teaching Machines to Improve Images
blocks.subtitle: Denoising, deblurring and super-resolution with neural networks

blocks.text:
A camera never records a perfect picture. Lenses blur, sensors add noise and small or distant cameras capture too few pixels. Image processing tries to undo that damage.

Classical methods used hand-designed filters. Neural networks instead learn, from many examples, what clean images look like and how to recover them.

blocks.heading: Restoration as an inverse problem
blocks.text: A degraded image can be modelled as a clean image that was blurred, reduced in size, and then corrupted by noise. Restoration runs this process backward. Because many clean images could have produced the same degraded one, the problem is **ill-posed**, and the network must supply plausible detail from what it has learned.

steps.text: **Degrade.** Training pairs are made by taking sharp images and applying blur, downsampling, noise and compression to imitate a real camera.
**Learn.** A network receives the degraded image and predicts the clean one. A loss function scores the difference and the weights are adjusted.
**Restore.** At run time the trained network maps a new low-quality image to a restored one in a single forward pass.
**Measure.** Results are judged with fidelity metrics such as PSNR and SSIM, with perceptual metrics, and by how well later tasks perform.

blocks.heading: Fidelity versus appearance
blocks.text: Networks trained only to minimise pixel error give high PSNR but smooth, slightly soft results. Adding **perceptual** and **adversarial** losses yields sharper, more convincing texture, at the risk of inventing detail that was never in the scene. For scientific, forensic or surveillance use, that trade-off must be stated openly.

items.title: Super-resolution
items.text: Estimating a high-resolution image from one or more low-resolution inputs.

items.title: PSNR
items.text: Peak signal-to-noise ratio: a logarithmic measure of pixel error against a reference.

items.title: SSIM
items.text: Structural similarity: compares local brightness, contrast and structure.

items.title: Pruning
items.text: Removing filters or weights that contribute little, to shrink and speed up a network.

items.title: Knowledge distillation
items.text: Training a small 'student' network to imitate a large 'teacher'.

blocks.heading: From the laboratory to the edge
blocks.text: The best models are large and slow. Drones, phones and embedded cameras need networks that run in real time on limited power. Pruning, quantisation, distillation and efficient architectures cut cost, and each must be checked for its effect on quality. Models also degrade on images unlike their training data.

items.title: Remote sensing
items.text: Sharper satellite and aerial imagery for mapping and monitoring.

items.title: Medical imaging
items.text: Lower-dose scans restored to diagnostic quality.

items.title: Photography
items.text: Night modes and digital zoom in phone cameras.

items.title: Surveillance
items.text: Clearer detail for detection and recognition tasks.

blocks.question: Why is single-image super-resolution called 'ill-posed'?
options: It needs a lot of memory
Many different high-resolution images reduce to the same low-resolution image
It only works on grey images
blocks.explanation: Information is lost in downsampling, so the inverse has no unique answer. The network chooses a plausible one.

blocks.question: A model trained only with pixel-wise error tends to give results that are:
options: High in PSNR but somewhat smooth
blocks.explanation: Minimising average pixel error favours the mean of plausible answers, which looks soft.

blocks.heading: Key terms and next steps
blocks.text:
**Degradation model**: the assumed blur, downsampling and noise. **Receptive field**: the input region that influences one output pixel. **Quantisation**: using fewer bits per weight. **Hallucination**: plausible but invented detail.
